newsitem.title: UK: INSTANT VIEW - UK Sept M4 money supply data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - UK Sept M4 money supply data.

text.p: Following is a selection of economists' reactions to UK M4 money supply and bank and building society lending data published at 0830 GMT.
September M4 money supply rose 0.8 percent m-m, and 9.8 percent y-y. Sept M4 bank and b/s lending up 3.5 bln stg.
"The bottom line to M4 is perhaps a little stronger than most people had anticipated."

"As far as the gilt-edged money market is concerned, they will take some heart from what appears at least on the surface to be a somewhat softer than anticipated private sector lending, particularly coming from the housing sector."

"I think the PSBR being firmer than expected has something to do with the higher headline figure. It is a bit worrying that we're back towards the 10 percent level, having seen that short-term dip to nine percent. But as the Treasury says, the actual figures are quite difficult to assess. With lending soft this month, mortgages also, and the BBA saying things are soft on the industrial and commercial companies side, I think the underlying picture is still a bit cloudy."

"It's bang in line with the market in terms of the aggregate. The real surprise is on the bank and building society lending, which is down on what the market was looking for. I think it's one off rather than an underlying shift downward. It's another indicator the economy is picking up. M4 money supply continues to support Eddie George's case for a rate rise...and he will certainly use it in the monthly meeting in his call for a rate rise."

"The M4 figures are a little worrying in that they are pointing in the same direction as figures for the real economy. The most interesting aspect of the series in recent months has been the growth in corporate borrowing, which has lately been mirrored in the personal sector -- not surprising given the strength in the housing market. Lending looks set to pick up further as the housing market stays firm and consumers seem not adverse to taking on more debt."
